```{=html}
<div class="c1-top">
<div class="lx-card lx-cap-brief">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The brief</p>
<p class="lx-case-q">Prairie Campus's board must choose a microgrid that keeps electricity flowing to the county hospital, its water and heating plant and the dorms through a three-day winter storm, within the host <span class="lx-term" data-term="feeder">feeder</span>'s limits.</p>
<p class="lx-hint c1-assume">Assume that powering these loads keeps their heating equipment working: heat demand and indoor temperature are not modeled.</p>
<ol class="lx-studio-task">
<li><b>Hand in:</b> a plan link and a one-page note with the annual cost, the unserved critical load, the emissions, a comparison of three owners and a sensitivity line (Modeler version: the M5 notebook too).</li>
<li><b>From:</b> the <a href="sb1-microgrid-workbench.html">Microgrid Workbench</a>'s engine and a hypothetical outage from 20 to 22 January 2025 (a teaching solar profile, a fictional campus).</li>
<li><b>Done when:</b> every check under the note is in place, the brief's three loads served among them, and the self-check reaches Proficient on every competence.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-hint">About 90 minutes: 35 to build and run the plan, 35 to write the note, 20 to check it.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-real c1-realworld">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:campus-resilience-question"><p>In an industry internship, the course author worked on this question: how should solar <span class="lx-term" data-term="photovoltaic">PV</span>, battery storage and backup generation be sized for an industrial campus to meet demand through grid outages?</p><p>The work used a <span class="lx-term" data-term="techno-economic-analysis">techno-economic</span> optimization model to size a resilient microgrid for the campus.</p><p>The company's data, models and results are confidential and are not shown here.</p></blockquote>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:supply-chain-mg"><p>From the course author's research: in the modeled supply chains, each open factory or warehouse could run its own microgrid, with on-site wind, solar and storage, an energy balance every hour, and energy bought from and sold to the grid.</p><p>Holds when: stylized networks with synthetic distances and costs, candidate sites in California, Arizona and Nevada, and one year, planned week by week for products and hour by hour for energy. Leaves out: grid outages, which the studies do not model.</p><footer>From: Li et al. (2023), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apm.2023.02.014">Applied Mathematical Modelling</a>.</footer></blockquote>
<p class="lx-hint">The full case: <a href="cf1-supply-chain-microgrids.html">case file CF1</a>.</p>
</div>
</div>

## Write your one-page note
:::

```{=html}
<div id="c1-note" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- c1-note:start -->
<ol class="lx-rn-outline"><li><b>Title and plan link:</b> the plan's link from the bench, and the date</li><li><b>Recommendation:</b> Two or three sentences: what to build, what stays on, and why.</li><li><b>The plan:</b> each choice, with its unit</li><li><b>Results:</b> each result, with its unit and boundary</li><li><b>Assumptions:</b> one sentence each</li><li><b>Sensitivity:</b> how one result moves when one input changes, and whether the plan was held fixed</li><li><b>Owner, and who pays:</b> One or two sentences: which owner, who pays, who decides.</li><li><b>What the plan cannot do:</b> One or two sentences: what could still leave the hospital short.</li><li><b>Limits of this analysis:</b> what the model leaves out</li></ol>
<!-- c1-note:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

## Check your note
:::

```{=html}
<div id="exemplars" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- c1-exemplars:start -->
<div class="lx-ex-cols">
<div class="lx-ex-ans weak"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Weak note · Developing</p><p class="lx-ex-lines">Build a big battery and lots of solar [1] so the hospital stays on. It will pay for itself [2], and the campus will be resilient [3].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Falls short:</b> No sizes and no units: the board cannot price or check it.</li><li value="2"><b>Falls short:</b> No number, no boundary, no dollar year: pays against what, over what time?</li><li value="3"><b>Falls short:</b> Resilient against which outage? Say the scenario and what the plan cannot survive.</li></ol></div>
<div class="lx-ex-ans good"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Strong note · Proficient</p><p class="lx-ex-lines"><b>Recommendation:</b> build 3,225 kW of solar, a 5,050 kWh battery and 2 generator sets with 675 gallons of diesel [1]. It keeps the hospital, the water and heating plant and the dorms powered for all 72 hours of the storm (0 kWh short).
<b>Cost:</b> $1,181,114 a year, community-owned, 2025 dollars: equipment, upkeep and the normal-year grid bill [2], $224,472 below the grid-only bill. The storm's 675 gallons of diesel ($2,470) are extra [3].
<b>Sensitivity:</b> 0 kWh short for a storm of 1 to 3 days, but 4,508 kWh on a fourth day, the plan held fixed [4].
<b>Emissions:</b> 6.9 t of CO₂ from the storm's diesel; 1,645 t from a normal year's grid electricity (U.S. average, operating only) [5].
<b>Assumptions:</b> a full battery and tank when the storm starts, the coming sun known, flat loads; powering the loads keeps their heating working, as heat is not modeled [6].
<b>Owner:</b> community. A co-op would pay $1,124,657 a year for the same plan, a utility $1,240,076. Community ownership costs $56,457 a year more than a co-op; it lets the campus and its neighbours set outage priorities themselves, a control I assume the board values above that [7].
<b>Limits:</b> one storm tested; a set that fails to start, how fuel use changes below full output and fuel deliveries are left out [8].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Works:</b> Sizes with units, and the fuel that limits the sets.</li><li value="2"><b>Works:</b> The cost with its boundary and dollar year (illustrative costs).</li><li value="3"><b>Works:</b> Storm fuel stated on its own: adding it to an annual cost would need an outage frequency.</li><li value="4"><b>Works:</b> The sensitivity, with the plan held fixed: the plan's limit, said plainly.</li><li value="5"><b>Works:</b> Emissions with their boundary: operating CO₂, average factor.</li><li value="6"><b>Works:</b> The assumptions that flatter the plan, named, with the brief's heating qualification.</li><li value="7"><b>Works:</b> Who pays and who decides, and the assumed benefit that justifies the premium: a reasoned choice, not the cheapest by default.</li><li value="8"><b>Works:</b> What the analysis leaves out, so the board does not over-read it.</li></ol></div>
</div>
<!-- c1-exemplars:end -->
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-fallback">

who pays named.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Costs and emissions on different boundaries.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Cost and emissions on one boundary; emissions question named; who pays and who benefits named.</td><td data-l="Strong">Distributional and environmental side effects estimated with stated assumptions.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Uncertainty<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: The sensitivity line: what a shorter or longer storm does to the plan held fixed.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Single numbers, or a storm length changed without the plan held fixed.</td><td data-l="Proficient">The sensitivity line: the unserved critical load for storms of 1, 2 and 4 days, the plan held fixed.</td><td data-l="Strong">Also names the storm length at which the plan first falls short, and what would buy that margin.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Realism<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: What the plan leaves out: fuel deliveries, a set that fails to start, how fuel use changes below full output.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Assumes fuel arrives, every set starts, or the storm is the only outage that matters.</td><td data-l="Proficient">What the plan leaves out (fuel deliveries, a set that fails to start, fuel use below full output) and the brief's heating assumption.</td><td data-l="Strong">Also checks one key input against its source, or a second source.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Communication<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: A page the campus's owner can act on: the recommendation first, then the numbers that back it.</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Results without limits.</td><td data-l="Proficient">A one-page note with the plan link: the recommendation first, then the evidence (the annual cost, the storm's unserved load and diesel CO₂), the storm-length sensitivity and the plan's limits.</td><td data-l="Strong">A briefing a decision-maker could act on without misreading.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

<tr><td>The storm</td><td class="n">72 hours</td><td class="s">From 00:00 on 20 January 2025, the grid assumed down; solar: a teaching profile from SPP's observed hourly solar (<a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">EIA-930</a> · accessed 2 Nov 2026), scaled to monthly capacity factors</td></tr>
<tr><td>Must stay on (to start)</td><td class="n">650 kW</td><td class="s">Hospital 300, water and heating plant 100, dorms 250 kW: F7's campus (illustrative)</td></tr>
<tr><td>Tariff level</td><td class="n">13.37¢/kWh</td><td class="s"><a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_02_04.html">EIA, Electric Power Annual, Table 2.4</a>, U.S. commercial average, 2025 · accessed 3 Nov 2026</td></tr>
<tr><td>CO₂ from diesel · from the grid</td><td class="n">10.19 kg/gal · 0.367 kg/kWh</td><td class="s"><a href="https://www.eia.gov/environment/emissions/co2_vol_mass.php">EIA coefficients</a> · <a href="https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=74&amp;t=11">EIA FAQ</a> (2023 U.S. average)</td></tr>
<tr><td>Owners' real <span class="lx-term" data-term="cost-of-capital">cost of capital</span></td><td class="n">6% · 4% · 5%</td><td class="s">Illustrative: utility, co-op, community</td></tr>
